tagline: An old stage route links village landmarks with Manchester’s water supply
intro: The Old Stagecoach Scenic Byway follows NH 121 through southern New Hampshire villages toward Massabesic Lake. Its 22 miles form one part of the 43-mile Robert Frost-Old Stagecoach Byway. Visit NH presents the combined drive through its woodlands, villages, farmsteads and orchards, with rural history and culture as the connecting theme. NH 121 winds through these communities; in Hampstead it takes the local names Main Street and Stage Road.

The route follows a stagecoach journey more than 200 years old, once connecting Boston and Concord. That early transport network supplies the byway's historical thread. In Atkinson, 3.74 miles of Main Street received the Stage Coach Byway name through the New Hampshire Scenic and Cultural Byways program in 2011. The adjoining Robert Frost segment brings a different focus, following the landscape of the poet's Derry years, from 1900 to 1911.

Travel northwest from Atkinson through Hampstead, where the Robert Frost segment reconnects with NH 121. Continue to Chester, whose village cemetery lies at the meeting of Routes 102 and 121. Auburn follows, then Massabesic Lake at the end of the byway. The lake serves as Manchester's drinking-water supply, and trails along its edge offer views of the water and Auburn.

moments.title: Atkinson
moments.text: Atkinson Academy's 1803 building replaced a schoolhouse destroyed by fire the year before. The institution itself began in 1787 as a boys' school, founded by Stephen Peabody, Nathaniel Peabody and William Cogswell, and admitted girls from 1791. The surviving building is a work of master builder Ebenezer Clifford. Its clapboarded, two-story front carries a tower with an open octagonal belfry and cupola. Modern wings extend behind it, giving the school a rough W shape. Pilasters and a pedimented gable set apart the three central bays of its seven-bay facade.

moments.title: Chester Village Cemetery
moments.text: Names on Chester's gravestones can identify the maker as well as the person buried. The cemetery has an unusually large number of markers signed by their carvers, including work by Stephen and Abel Webster. Those signatures helped researchers distinguish the two men's styles and identify their stones in other regional cemeteries. Established in 1751, the ground became Chester's main burial place, and families moved remains here from smaller plots and churchyards. The oldest section, the Revolutionary Quarter, runs along Route 121. Its monuments are chiefly slate or sandstone, with some marble; Abel Webster himself is buried here.
moments.notice: The Revolutionary Quarter along Route 121 contains mainly slate and sandstone monuments, with some marble.

moments.title: Massabesic Lake
moments.text: Massabesic supplies Manchester with drinking water, a role that shapes recreation on the lake. Swimming and water skiing are prohibited, while sailing, fishing and kayaking are popular. The lake covers about 2,560 acres across Manchester and Auburn, with recreational trails offering views of the water and town. Its name derives from the Abenaki Massa'nbesek, meaning “at the great water” or “to the great pond.” Water also leaves the lake through Cohas Brook, then flows toward the Merrimack River. The byway ends at this lake, where a water supply and a place for recreation share the same shoreline.
